contrast: Don't mix up *Nigerian* (from Nigeria) with *Nigerien* (from Niger, a different country, said nee-ZHAIR-ee-uhn).

senses.gloss: Of or from Nigeria, its people or its culture.
examples: The *Nigerian* film industry is one of the biggest in the world.
My roommate is *Nigerian* — he grew up in Lagos.
We ate at a *Nigerian* restaurant in Houston.

form: -ing from the verb *niggle*, to bother in a small way

senses.gloss: Small but annoying, and hard to stop thinking about.
senses.ru: мелкий, но докучливый; не дающий покоя
examples: I had a *niggling* doubt about the contract.
A *niggling* pain in his knee kept him out of the game.
There was something *niggling* about the way she said goodbye.

senses.gloss: Frightening or awful, like a bad dream.
examples: Traffic downtown was *nightmarish* all afternoon.
The movie ends with a *nightmarish* chase through the subway.
Losing your passport abroad is a *nightmarish* experience.

senses.gloss: Believing that nothing has meaning or value.
examples: His later poems take a *nihilistic* view of history.
The band's lyrics are darkly *nihilistic*.
She dismissed the plan as *nihilistic* and pointless.

senses.gloss: Able to move quickly and lightly.
examples: The cat was *nimble* enough to land on the narrow ledge.
Her fingers are *nimbler* than mine on the keyboard.
You need *nimble* feet to play that position.

senses.gloss: Quick to think or to change direction.
examples: He has a *nimble* mind and never loses an argument.
A *nimble* startup can change direction in a week.

position: both — mostly after a verb: *it's nippy out*
contrast: Informal, and only for mildly cold air — never for a freezing day or for a cold person. You say *it's nippy*, not "I'm nippy".

senses.gloss: Cold enough to make you want a jacket.
examples: It's *nippy* out there this morning.
October evenings get *nippier* every week.
Bring a sweater — the wind off the lake is *nippy*.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a no-frills airline*

senses.gloss: Offering only the basics, with nothing extra.
examples: We flew on a *no-frills* airline to Denver.
It's a *no-frills* motel, but it's clean and cheap.
The gym sells a *no-frills* membership for fifteen dollars a month.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a no-go zone*
contrast: As a noun *a no-go* means something that will not happen: *The merger is a no-go*. The adjective stays in front of a noun: *a no-go area*.

senses.gloss: That people are not allowed to enter, or are afraid to.
examples: The street became a *no-go* area after dark.
That side of the park is a *no-go* zone for dogs.
The old server room is treated as *no-go* territory.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a no-good liar*
contrast: Informal and insulting, and it needs the hyphen. Without one, *no good* is an ordinary phrase after a verb: *That plan is no good*.

senses.gloss: Worthless or dishonest.
examples: Her *no-good* ex-husband never paid a dime of support.
He fell in with a bunch of *no-good* kids.
That *no-good* car broke down twice in one week.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a no-nonsense boss*

senses.gloss: Practical and direct, with no time wasted.
examples: She's a *no-nonsense* manager who starts meetings on time.
The book gives *no-nonsense* advice about money.
He had a *no-nonsense* haircut and plain wire glasses.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a no-win situation*

senses.gloss: Such that every choice leads to a bad result.
examples: Fire him or keep him — it's a *no-win* situation.
The coach was in a *no-win* position with the press.
Arguing with your landlord about this is a *no-win* proposition.

contrast: *Nocturnal* belongs to animals and to formal or medical writing. For an ordinary evening plan say *at night* or *a nighttime walk*.

senses.gloss: Of an animal: active at night and asleep by day.
examples: Owls and raccoons are *nocturnal*.
Bats are *nocturnal* hunters that find insects by sound.
The zoo built a dark room for its *nocturnal* animals.

senses.gloss: Happening during the night.
examples: *Nocturnal* noise from the bar keeps the neighbors up.
The doctor asked about his *nocturnal* trips to the bathroom.

senses.gloss: Making no sound at all.
examples: The new dishwasher is almost *noiseless*.
He made a *noiseless* exit through the back door.
Electric buses are nearly *noiseless* at low speed.

senses.gloss: Of a people who move from place to place instead of settling.
examples: The region was home to *nomadic* herders for centuries.
*Nomadic* tribes followed the rain across the plateau.

senses.gloss: Of a life: spent moving around a lot.
examples: After college she led a *nomadic* life, moving every few months.
Consulting work makes for a *nomadic* existence.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *the nominal head*
contrast: In economics it has a third job: *nominal* wages are the dollar figure before inflation, *real* wages the figure after it.

senses.gloss: Holding a title but not the real power.
examples: He is the *nominal* head of the company, but his daughter runs it.
The vice president is the *nominal* chair of the board.
She stayed the *nominal* owner for another two years.

senses.gloss: Of an amount: so small it hardly counts.
examples: There's a *nominal* fee of five dollars.
They charge a *nominal* amount for shipping.

senses.gloss: Fixed, and not open to discussion or change.
examples: The deadline is *non-negotiable*.
Safety rules are a *non-negotiable* part of the job.
He made it clear that the price was *non-negotiable*.

contrast: A word of statistics and official reports. In ordinary American speech people name the group — *Black*, *Latino*, *Asian American* — or say *people of color*.

senses.gloss: Belonging to a racial group other than white.
examples: *Non-white* students make up half of the freshman class.
The neighborhood was almost entirely *non-white* in 1970.
The report splits the data into white and *non-white* households.

senses.gloss: Containing no alcohol.
examples: They always have a *nonalcoholic* option at the bar.
The punch is *nonalcoholic*, so the kids can have some.
*Nonalcoholic* beer has gotten much better in the last few years.

senses.gloss: Not taking the side of any big power or party.
examples: India led the *nonaligned* countries during the Cold War.
The small republic stayed *nonaligned* for decades.
He writes for a *nonaligned* paper with no party ties.

senses.gloss: Calm and relaxed about something other people would worry about.
examples: He was surprisingly *nonchalant* about losing his wallet.
She gave a *nonchalant* shrug and walked away.
Try to look *nonchalant* when you walk past the guard.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *noncombatant personnel*
contrast: More often a noun — *civilian noncombatants* — and as an adjective it stays in front of the noun.

senses.gloss: Not taking part in the fighting of a war.
examples: *Noncombatant* personnel were flown out first.
He served in a *noncombatant* role as a medic.
The treaty is meant to protect *noncombatant* civilians.

senses.gloss: Not run for profit and not carrying advertising.
examples: The station is *noncommercial* and runs on donations.
You may use the photo for *noncommercial* purposes.
*Noncommercial* radio carries no ads at all.

ru: уклончивый, ни к чему не обязывающий

senses.gloss: Careful not to say what you think or what you will do.
examples: The senator was *noncommittal* about the bill.
I got a *noncommittal* "we'll see" from my dad.
She stayed *noncommittal* until she had seen the numbers.

ru: не соблюдающий правила; не соответствующий требованиям

senses.gloss: Of a person: not following the rules or the treatment given.
examples: The patient was *noncompliant* with his medication.
*Noncompliant* drivers get a written warning first.

senses.gloss: Of a thing: not meeting a standard or a code.
examples: Three of the buildings are *noncompliant* with the fire code.
The inspector found *noncompliant* wiring in the basement.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *nonconformist views*
contrast: Far more common as a noun: *He was always a nonconformist*. The adjective stays in front of the noun.

senses.gloss: Refusing to follow what most people think or do.
examples: She had *nonconformist* views about schooling.
The gallery shows *nonconformist* art from the 1970s.
His *nonconformist* streak got him in trouble at work.

senses.gloss: Not passed from one person to another.
examples: The rash is *noncontagious*, so she can go to school.
Diabetes is a *noncontagious* disease.
They moved him to a *noncontagious* ward.

senses.gloss: Not likely to make anyone argue.
examples: The mayor opened with a *noncontroversial* proposal about the parks.
Repaving the road was *noncontroversial*.
They picked the most *noncontroversial* candidate they could find.

senses.gloss: Not tied to any one branch of a religion.
examples: It's a *nondenominational* chapel, open to everyone.
They had a *nondenominational* wedding ceremony.
The hospital chaplain's service is *nondenominational*.

senses.gloss: So ordinary that there is nothing to describe.
examples: He drove a *nondescript* gray sedan.
The office is in a *nondescript* building on Third Street.
Her handwriting is neat but *nondescript*.

senses.gloss: Not necessary, though possibly useful.
examples: *Nonessential* travel was canceled during the storm.
The store closed its *nonessential* departments.
Everything left in that box is *nonessential*.

ru: не освобождённый (от налога, от оплаты сверхурочных)
contrast: An American workplace and tax word. A *nonexempt* employee has to be paid overtime; an *exempt* one is on salary and is not.

senses.gloss: Not freed from a rule, a tax or a payment that others escape.
examples: *Nonexempt* employees clock in and out.
Her position is *nonexempt*, so she gets time and a half.
The form asks whether any of the property is *nonexempt*.

senses.gloss: Not there at all, or so small it might as well not be.
examples: Cell service out there is basically *nonexistent*.
He complained about a *nonexistent* charge on his bill.
My free time this month is *nonexistent*.

contrast: On American labels *nonfat* and *fat-free* mean the same thing. *Low-fat* is different — it still has some fat.

senses.gloss: Of a food, especially milk: with the fat taken out.
examples: She orders a *nonfat* latte every morning.
The yogurt is *nonfat* but still creamy.
We only buy *nonfat* milk.

senses.gloss: Serious but not causing death.
examples: He walked away with *nonfatal* injuries.
The crash was serious but *nonfatal*.
The report counts both fatal and *nonfatal* accidents.

contrast: In everyday American English people say *a nonfiction book*, using the noun. *Nonfictional* is rarer and sounds academic.

senses.gloss: Describing real events and people, not invented ones.
examples: The class reads both novels and *nonfictional* texts.
It is a *nonfictional* account of the 1906 earthquake.
Her later work is entirely *nonfictional*.

contrast: A famous trap: *flammable* and *inflammable* both mean "catches fire easily" — the *in-* is not a negative. The real opposite of both is *nonflammable*.

senses.gloss: That will not catch fire easily.
examples: The curtains are made of *nonflammable* fabric.
Store the paint in a *nonflammable* cabinet.
The label says the cleaner is *nonflammable*.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *nonhuman primates*

senses.gloss: Belonging to a species other than our own.
senses.ru: относящийся не к человеку, а к другим видам
examples: The study looked at *nonhuman* primates.
The lab tests the drug on *nonhuman* subjects first.
Science fiction is full of *nonhuman* characters.

senses.gloss: Of a test or treatment: done without cutting into the body.
examples: An MRI is a *noninvasive* test.
They tried *noninvasive* treatment first.
The clinic offers a *noninvasive* way to check blood sugar.

senses.gloss: Of a plant or animal: not spreading and crowding out what was there.
examples: The nursery sells only *noninvasive* ground cover.
Choose a *noninvasive* vine for the fence.

contrast: American spelling has no *e* after the *g*: *nonjudgmental*. British writing uses *non-judgemental*.

senses.gloss: Listening without criticizing or blaming.
examples: She listened in a warm, *nonjudgmental* way.
The group is meant to be a *nonjudgmental* space.
Try to be *nonjudgmental* when he tells you.

senses.gloss: Not meant or able to kill.
examples: Police used *nonlethal* weapons to break up the crowd.
Rubber bullets are supposed to be *nonlethal*.
The dose was high but *nonlethal*.

senses.gloss: Of a relationship or an equation: not changing at a steady rate.
examples: The relationship between dose and effect is *nonlinear*.
*Nonlinear* equations are much harder to solve.

senses.gloss: Of a story: not told in the order the events happened.
examples: The film has a *nonlinear* plot that jumps around in time.
She writes in a *nonlinear* style that takes getting used to.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *nonliving matter*

senses.gloss: Not alive, and never was.
examples: Students sort the samples into living and *nonliving* things.
Soil holds living organisms and *nonliving* matter together.
A virus sits on the line between living and *nonliving* material.

senses.gloss: Not connected with armed forces or war.
examples: The package includes *nonmilitary* aid only.
They hit *nonmilitary* targets near the border.
Most of the department's spending is *nonmilitary*.

contrast: Often written *non-native*. For people it describes the language, not the person: *a nonnative speaker*, not "a nonnative".

senses.gloss: Speaking a language learned later, not from birth.
senses.ru: неноситель языка, говорящий на неродном языке
examples: The course is for *nonnative* speakers of English.
His accent marks him as *nonnative*.

senses.gloss: Of a plant or animal: brought in from somewhere else.
examples: Kudzu is a *nonnative* plant in the South.
*Nonnative* fish have crowded out the trout.

senses.gloss: Not supporting any political party.
senses.ru: не связанный ни с одной партией
examples: The budget commission is *nonpartisan*.
She works for a *nonpartisan* think tank.
The city holds *nonpartisan* elections, with no party labels on the ballot.

contrast: Two opposite meanings fight over this word in America. The old one is "too confused to react"; many Americans now use it for "completely unbothered". Since your reader may take it either way, *puzzled* or *unfazed* is safer.

senses.gloss: So surprised or confused that you do not know how to react.
examples: She was completely *nonplussed* by the question.
He stood there *nonplussed*, holding the empty box.
The interviewer looked *nonplussed* for the first time all night.

senses.gloss: Not containing poison and safe to touch or eat.
examples: Most snakes in this state are *nonpoisonous*.
Look for a *nonpoisonous* houseplant if you have cats.
The mushroom is *nonpoisonous* but tastes terrible.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *nonprescription drugs*
contrast: *Over-the-counter* is the everyday American phrase for the same thing.

senses.gloss: Sold without a doctor's note.
examples: You can buy *nonprescription* pain relievers anywhere.
The store has a whole aisle of *nonprescription* remedies.
Ask the pharmacist about *nonprescription* options.

senses.gloss: Not done for a living, or not trained for pay.
examples: The tournament is open to *nonprofessional* players.
He sings in a *nonprofessional* choir on Sundays.
*Nonprofessional* volunteers handled the phones all night.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a nonprofit group*
contrast: Also a noun in American English: *She works for a nonprofit*. British writing says *non-profit-making*.

senses.gloss: Set up to do good work rather than to make money.
examples: She runs a *nonprofit* organization in Chicago.
The hospital has *nonprofit* status.
Several *nonprofit* groups filed the lawsuit.

senses.gloss: Of a resource: used up for good once it is gone.
examples: Coal and oil are *nonrenewable* resources.
They're moving away from *nonrenewable* energy.

senses.gloss: Of a contract or permit: not able to be extended.
examples: The grant is *nonrenewable* after five years.
It's a one-year, *nonrenewable* appointment.

contrast: Also a noun. It turns up all over American paperwork: *nonresident tuition*, *a nonresident fishing license*.

senses.gloss: Not living in the state, country or place in question.
senses.ru: не проживающий в данном штате или стране
examples: *Nonresident* students pay higher tuition.
He filed a *nonresident* tax return in two states.
The rate is different if you're *nonresident*.

senses.gloss: Not meant for people to live in.
examples: The building is in a *nonresidential* part of town.
The lot is zoned *nonresidential*.
*Nonresidential* construction picked up last quarter.

senses.gloss: That you cannot bring back or get money for.
examples: All sale items are *nonreturnable*.
The deposit is *nonreturnable* once work begins.
It came in a *nonreturnable* bottle.

senses.gloss: Not belonging to or favoring one religious group.
examples: It's a *nonsectarian* school with students of every faith.
The charity is *nonsectarian*.
They hold a *nonsectarian* memorial service each spring.

senses.gloss: Making no sense; silly or absurd.
examples: His explanation was completely *nonsensical*.
The instructions were translated badly and came out *nonsensical*.
She told the kids a *nonsensical* rhyme about a purple cow.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a nonslip mat*

senses.gloss: Made so that it will not slide or let you slide.
examples: Put a *nonslip* mat in the tub.
The boots have a thick *nonslip* sole.
We laid *nonslip* tile in the kitchen.

senses.gloss: Of language: not the form used in schools and formal writing.
examples: "Ain't" is considered *nonstandard*.
*Nonstandard* English is not bad English, just different English.

senses.gloss: Not the usual size, shape or type.
examples: The window is a *nonstandard* size, so it has to be ordered.
They charge extra for *nonstandard* parts.

senses.gloss: Coated so that food does not stick to it.
examples: Use a *nonstick* pan for the eggs.
The coating is *nonstick* and wipes clean.
I bought a set of *nonstick* baking sheets.

contrast: Also an adverb: *We flew nonstop to Miami*, *She talked nonstop*. As an adjective it sits in front of the noun: *a nonstop flight*.

senses.gloss: Of a trip: going the whole way without stopping.
examples: Is there a *nonstop* flight to Denver?
We took the *nonstop* train and got in by noon.

senses.gloss: Going on and on without a break.
examples: It was *nonstop* rain for three days.
The phones have been *nonstop* since the ad ran.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *nonsurgical treatment*

senses.gloss: Treating a problem without an operation.
examples: They tried a *nonsurgical* approach first.
*Nonsurgical* options include physical therapy and rest.
She's looking into *nonsurgical* treatments for her back.

senses.gloss: That no tax has to be paid on.
examples: The reimbursement is *nontaxable*.
Some *nontaxable* income still has to be reported.
Gifts under that amount are *nontaxable*.

senses.gloss: Using plain words that someone outside the field can follow.
examples: Can you explain it in *nontechnical* terms?
The manual is written for a *nontechnical* reader.
His questions were mostly *nontechnical*.

senses.gloss: Not poisonous or harmful to touch or breathe.
examples: The paint is water-based and *nontoxic*.
Look for *nontoxic* cleaning products.
These crayons are *nontoxic* and safe for toddlers.

senses.gloss: Not following the usual custom or pattern.
examples: They had a *nontraditional* wedding on the beach.
The college enrolls many *nontraditional* students in their thirties and forties.
His career path has been *nontraditional* from the start.

senses.gloss: That only the named person may use.
examples: The ticket is *nontransferable*.
It's a *nontransferable* membership.
The prize is *nontransferable* and has no cash value.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *nonunion labor*

senses.gloss: Not belonging to, or not using, a labor union.
examples: The plant hired *nonunion* labor.
He works at a *nonunion* shop across the river.
*Nonunion* drivers make less per mile.

senses.gloss: Not using words.
examples: Much of what we tell each other is *nonverbal*.
She's good at reading *nonverbal* cues.
The test measures *nonverbal* reasoning.

senses.gloss: Using or involving no force against people.
examples: King led a *nonviolent* protest movement.
The demonstration stayed *nonviolent* all afternoon.
He was convicted of a *nonviolent* offense.

contrast: *Nordic* takes in Finland and Iceland as well; *Scandinavian* strictly means Denmark, Norway and Sweden.

senses.gloss: Of the countries of northern Europe, their people or their style.
examples: The *Nordic* countries are Denmark, Norway, Sweden, Finland and Iceland.
*Nordic* design is known for clean lines and pale wood.
Her features are strikingly *Nordic*.

senses.gloss: Of cross-country skiing and the events that go with it.
examples: She competes in *Nordic* skiing, not downhill.
The resort has forty miles of *Nordic* trails.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *Norse mythology*
contrast: Almost always in *Old Norse* (the language) and *Norse mythology*. For Norway today the word is *Norwegian*.

senses.gloss: Of the medieval Scandinavians, their language or their myths.
examples: *Norse* mythology gave us the names of several weekdays.
Old *Norse* words fill English: *sky*, *knife*, *they*.
The museum has a *Norse* ship burial on display.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *the north side*
contrast: In *drive north* it is an adverb and in *the North* a noun. *north* lives mostly in names and parts — *the north side*, *North Dakota* — while *northern* is the general word: *northern Michigan*, not "north Michigan".

senses.gloss: On, in or facing the north.
examples: Their apartment is on the *north* side of the building.
Take the *north* entrance to the garage.
The *north* wall never gets any sun.

senses.gloss: Of a wind: blowing from the north.
examples: A cold *north* wind blew all week.
*North* winds usually bring the first snow.

position: both — *North African food*, *Her family is North African*

senses.gloss: Of or from the north of Africa, its people or its culture.
examples: We ate at a *North African* restaurant in Brooklyn.
The band mixes jazz with *North African* rhythms.
Her grandparents are *North African*.

position: both — *the North American market*, *The species is North American*
contrast: *North American* covers Canada, the United States and Mexico. *American* on its own usually means only the United States.

senses.gloss: Of or from North America.
examples: The company's *North American* sales rose last year.
This bird is found only on the *North American* continent.
The plant is *North American* in origin.

position: both — *North Korean television*, *He is North Korean*

senses.gloss: Of or from North Korea or its people.
examples: The *North Korean* delegation arrived on Tuesday.
He studies *North Korean* politics.
The defector is *North Korean* by birth.

senses.gloss: Traveling toward the north.
examples: The *northbound* lanes are backed up for miles.
We caught the *northbound* train at noon.
Most of the morning traffic is *northbound*.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *the northeast corner*
contrast: Also an adverb (*head northeast*) and a noun (*the Northeast*). For a region and its people use *northeastern*.

senses.gloss: On, in or facing the northeast.
examples: The storm came in over the *northeast* corner of the lake.
There's a service door on the *northeast* side.
A *northeast* wind picked up after dark.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *northeastern states*

senses.gloss: Of or in the northeastern part of a country or region.
examples: She grew up in *northeastern* Ohio.
The *northeastern* states got two feet of snow.
It's a *northeastern* species of oak.

form: -ly from *north* — an adjective, not an adverb
contrast: Two traps. It ends in *-ly* but it is an adjective, so never "northerly-ly". And a *northerly* wind blows FROM the north, while a *northerly* course heads TOWARD it.

senses.gloss: Of a wind: coming from the north.
examples: A *northerly* breeze cooled things off by evening.
The wind turned *northerly* overnight.

senses.gloss: Lying toward or moving toward the north.
examples: They set a *northerly* course out of the harbor.
We took the more *northerly* of the two routes.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *the northernmost town*

senses.gloss: Farthest to the north.
examples: Utqiagvik is the *northernmost* town in the United States.
The *northernmost* point of the island is a bare cliff.
We camped at the *northernmost* site in the park.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *the northwest corner*
contrast: Also an adverb (*drive northwest*) and a noun (*the Pacific Northwest*). For a region use *northwestern*.

senses.gloss: On, in or facing the northwest.
examples: The *northwest* corner of the lot is still empty.
A *northwest* wind brought rain by morning.
Use the *northwest* stairwell during construction.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *northwestern forests*

senses.gloss: Of or in the northwestern part of a country or region.
examples: He teaches at a college in *northwestern* Montana.
*Northwestern* forests are full of Douglas fir.
It's a *northwestern* dialect you rarely hear back east.

contrast: Russian *ностальгия* often means missing home; English *nostalgic* is about missing a time, not a place. For missing home say *homesick*.

senses.gloss: Feeling a warm sadness about a time in the past.
examples: He gets *nostalgic* about college every fall.
I'm *nostalgic* for the old neighborhood.

senses.gloss: Of a thing: bringing that feeling back.
examples: The show has a *nostalgic* 1980s soundtrack.
There's something *nostalgic* about the smell of chalk.

ru: любопытный, сующий нос не в своё дело
contrast: American spelling is *nosy*; *nosey* is a British variant. Note it is always a complaint — for harmless interest say *curious*.

senses.gloss: Too interested in other people's private business.
examples: Our *nosy* neighbor watches everyone's mail.
Don't be *nosy* — it's none of your business.
The older she gets, the *nosier* she gets.

contrast: *Notable* means worth noticing; *noticeable* means big enough to be seen or heard. A *noticeable* stain, a *notable* achievement.

senses.gloss: Important or interesting enough to be worth mentioning.
examples: The most *notable* change is the new roof.
The town is *notable* for its covered bridge.

senses.gloss: Of a person: well known and respected.
examples: Several *notable* writers signed the letter.
She's a *notable* figure in her field.

form: -ed from the noun *notch*, a small cut

senses.gloss: Having a small V-shaped cut or cuts in the edge.
examples: The blade has a *notched* edge for cutting rope.
He wore a jacket with *notched* lapels.
The stick was *notched* every few inches.

position: both — before a noun (*a noted surgeon*), or after a verb with *for*
contrast: Before a noun, *noted* means famous. After a verb on its own it is just the past of *note*: *Your objection is noted* means it was written down, not that it is famous.

senses.gloss: Well known, especially for one particular thing.
examples: A *noted* historian gave the keynote address.
The valley is *noted* for its apples.
She's a *noted* authority on wetlands.

senses.gloss: Worth paying attention to.
examples: The *noteworthy* part is how fast they fixed it.
Nothing *noteworthy* happened all week.
Her essay makes several *noteworthy* points.

contrast: Keep the *e* in the middle: *noticeable*, never "noticable" — the *e* is what keeps the *c* soft.

senses.gloss: Easy to see, hear or feel.
examples: There's a *noticeable* dent in the door.
The difference is more *noticeable* in person.
His accent is barely *noticeable* now.

contrast: *Notorious* is famous for something bad. A great scientist is *famous*, never *notorious*. Say *a notorious intersection* only if it is known for crashes.

senses.gloss: Well known for something bad.
examples: He's *notorious* for showing up late.
The prison held some of the country's most *notorious* criminals.
That stretch of highway is *notorious*.

form: -ing — what the food does for you

senses.gloss: Full of what the body needs to stay healthy.
examples: A bowl of lentil soup is cheap and *nourishing*.
She made a *nourishing* stew that lasted all week.
Oatmeal is more *nourishing* than a donut.

contrast: A double false friend. The noun *novel* is a роман, a long book — and Russian *новелла* is a short story, not a novel at all. The adjective has nothing to do with books: it means new and original.

senses.gloss: New in a way nobody has tried before.
examples: She came up with a *novel* way to pay for it.
The idea was *novel* at the time.
It's a *novel* approach to a very old problem.

contrast: *Noxious* is harmful or foul-smelling — *noxious fumes*. *Obnoxious* is about a person being unbearable — *an obnoxious guest*. They are not related in meaning.

senses.gloss: Harmful or unpleasant to breathe, touch or live with.
examples: *Noxious* fumes drove everyone out of the building.
The state lists the plant as a *noxious* weed.
The smell coming from the drain was *noxious*.

contrast: The same word is also an adverb: *He caught it one-handed*. There it tells you how, not what kind.

senses.gloss: Done with or using only one hand.
examples: He made a *one-handed* catch at the fence.
There's a *one-handed* way to open the jar.
The drill is light enough for *one-handed* use.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a one-horse town*
contrast: Nearly always in *a one-horse town*, meaning a tiny, dull place. The literal sense — a wagon pulled by one horse — is long gone from daily speech.

senses.gloss: Small, poor and not worth much.
examples: He grew up in a *one-horse* town in Nebraska.
It's a *one-horse* operation — just him and a truck.
The place felt like a *one-horse* village after Chicago.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a one-man show*
contrast: *One-woman* and *one-person* work exactly the same way: *a one-woman show*, *a one-person operation*.

senses.gloss: Done, run or performed by a single person.
examples: The store is a *one-man* operation.
He put on a *one-man* show at the little theater downtown.
It was a *one-man* campaign against the new highway.

contrast: Also an adverb and a noun: *We met one-on-one*, *She asked for a one-on-one with the boss*.

senses.gloss: Between just two people.
examples: I had a *one-on-one* meeting with my manager.
The tutoring is *one-on-one*.
He's better in *one-on-one* conversation than in a group.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *one-party rule*

senses.gloss: Governed by a single political party, with no real opposition.
examples: It has been a *one-party* state for forty years.
*One-party* rule ended there in 1990.
The country held its first free vote after decades of *one-party* government.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a one-piece swimsuit*
contrast: Also a noun for the swimsuit itself: *She wore a one-piece*.

senses.gloss: Made in a single piece instead of separate parts.
examples: She bought a black *one-piece* swimsuit.
The baby was in a *one-piece* snowsuit.
The tub and surround come as a *one-piece* unit.

senses.gloss: Showing only one point of view; unfair.
examples: The article gives a very *one-sided* account of the strike.
His version of the fight is *one-sided*.

senses.gloss: So unequal that one side does all the work or all the winning.
senses.ru: неравный, с явным перевесом одной стороны
examples: The game was *one-sided* from the first quarter.
Their friendship is *one-sided* — she does all the calling.
It was the most *one-sided* election in years.
